overview.text: The Copperhead is a medium-sized pit viper of the eastern United States, named for its coppery head. Its pattern of hourglass-shaped bands makes it hard to spot among dead leaves. It is venomous, but it usually bites only if someone steps on it, grabs it or comes very close.

identification.text: A tan to pinkish snake with chestnut-brown or mahogany crossbands. Seen from above the bands are narrow in the middle of the back and wide on the sides, like an hourglass; sometimes they are broken in the middle.

size.label: Adults
size.text: Usually about 61 to 91 cm (24 to 36 in) long; northern adults are often 66 to 86 cm.

variation.label: Young
variation.text: Babies have a bright yellow tail tip, which they wiggle like a worm or caterpillar to lure frogs and lizards within striking range.

habitat.text: In many areas it lives in high, dry, rocky, well-wooded places dominated by oaks and hickories.

diet.text: Frogs, toads, lizards, insects and caterpillars, mice and birds.

reproduction.text: Gives birth to live young in late summer or autumn. Litters range from 2 to 17, usually 6 to 9; in Indiana, females give birth to 4 to 8 young every other year.

taxonomy.text: A 2015 genetic study proposed splitting the copperhead into two species: the Eastern Copperhead (*A. contortrix*) and the Broad-banded Copperhead (*A. laticinctus*) of the south-central United States.

funfacts.text: Baby copperheads use their yellow tail tips as fishing lures.
